entries.clue: Tourist concern about reenactment (14)

indicatorNotes.about: 'about' can mean moved around, so the letters are turned about into a new order

annotation.surface: A visitor frets over a historical re-enactment they have come to watch.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a preposition meaning 'regarding', but here it instructs you to turn the whole of 'tourist concern' about.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a staged version of a crime or battle acts it out again.

entries.clue: Criminal aunty nicks room somewhere in North America (5,9)

indicatorNotes.Criminal: something criminal is bent or crooked, so the letters are bent out of shape

annotation.surface: A light-fingered aunt steals a room somewhere on a North American trip.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nicks' (British slang for steals) and 'Criminal' dress the fodder up as a theft story, but every letter of 'aunty nicks room' is simply rearranged.
annotation.definitionFit: The Rocky Mountains are a range running through western Canada and the USA.

entries.clue: Firm in time gets currency (7)

blocks.note: an age = a period of time

annotation.surface: A company that holds on long enough ends up making money.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like an instruction to put one piece inside another, but here it is simply read as it stands.
annotation.definitionFit: Coinage is a country's system of coins, its currency.

entries.clue: Things upset Kitty in discothèque? (9)

indicatorNotes.upset: upset things are knocked over and out of order

blocks.note: a kitty or pot is a pool of money, as in poker

annotation.surface: Drinks knocked over and a cat underfoot at a disco.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Kitty' suggests a cat, but it is the pot of shared money. The question mark flags that a discothèque is just one kind of nightspot.
annotation.definitionFit: A nightspot is a club or venue for evening entertainment, such as a disco.

entries.clue: Follows Peg into dive (8)

blocks.note: to tail someone is to follow them
a peg and a pin both fix things in place

annotation.surface: Someone trails a woman called Peg into a seedy bar.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Peg' reads as a woman's name and 'dive' as a seedy bar; they are a pin and a steep descent.
annotation.definitionFit: A tailspin is a spinning plunge by an aircraft, a dive.

entries.clue: Alarms peacekeepers with article in manuscript (6)

indicatorNotes.in: one thing placed in another goes inside it

blocks.note: UN = United Nations, whose troops keep the peace
MS = manuscript; it holds AN, giving M-AN-S

annotation.surface: Soldiers of the peace force are rattled by a piece in a document.
annotation.walkthrough: To unman someone is to rob them of courage, so it fits 'alarms' more closely than it first appears.
annotation.definitionFit: Unmans means deprives of nerve, frightens: alarms.

entries.clue: Propose panel (5)

blocks.note: in British committee usage, to put a motion forward for discussion
a flat board or slab, as a stone or wooden panel is

annotation.surface: Put forward a committee.
annotation.walkthrough: In British usage, to table a motion is to propose it for discussion; in American usage it means the opposite, to shelve it.
annotation.definitionFit: Table is to propose (a motion) and also a flat panel of wood or stone.

entries.clue: Revealed rents for shops (7)

blocks.note: a secret that is out has been revealed
to let a flat is to rent it out

annotation.surface: Published figures show what retailers pay in rent.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rents' looks like a noun, but the charade needs the verb: a landlord lets property.
annotation.definitionFit: Retail jargon: a shop is a point of sale where goods flow out to customers.

entries.clue: Distribute merchant’s mushy plants (14)

indicatorNotes.Distribute: distributed things are spread about, so the letters are scattered into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters; the apostrophe S supplies an S

annotation.surface: An order to hand out a trader's wilting stock of plants.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'merchant's' possessive S counts as a letter of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the answer names one particular genus of flowering plant.

entries.clue: Food wrapping around fish with thin skin (5,4)

blocks.note: c = circa, Latin for around, as in c.1900
the ling is a sea fish
a film is a thin layer or skin

annotation.surface: Plastic wrap stretched round a thin-skinned fish fillet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Around' looks like a container indicator, but here it is C, for circa. Cling film is the British name for plastic wrap.
annotation.definitionFit: Cling film is the thin plastic sheet used to wrap food.

entries.clue: Tough yet outwardly childish (5)

indicatorNotes.outwardly: the outward part of a word is its first and last letters

blocks.note: yet and but both introduce a contrast
the outer letters of CHILDISH are C and H

annotation.surface: Someone who looks hard but is a big kid underneath.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Outwardly' reads as 'on the surface', but it means take the outside letters of 'childish'.
annotation.definitionFit: Butch means tough and aggressively masculine in manner.

entries.clue: Unknown direction for fungi (5)

annotation.definitionNote: 'fungi' is plural; yeast is a mass noun covering many single-celled fungi

blocks.note: x, y and z are the algebraic unknowns

annotation.surface: No one knows which way to go to find mushrooms.
annotation.walkthrough: Setters may use any of X, Y or Z for 'unknown'; here the crossing letters or the answer settle it as Y.
annotation.definitionFit: Yeasts are microscopic single-celled fungi.

entries.clue: From that time count honestly (9)

blocks.note: to count on someone is to rely on them

annotation.surface: Ever since then, tally everything up truthfully.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Count' looks like it means add up, but it is count as in 'count on', meaning rely.
annotation.definitionFit: To say something sincerely is to say it honestly.

entries.clue: Six deliveries by Penny and Grant more than amply rewarded (8)

blocks.note: in cricket an over is six balls bowled
a grant of money is aid

annotation.surface: A courier, Penny and Grant got well paid for six parcels.
annotation.walkthrough: Penny and Grant look like two people's names; they are P and AID. An over is a set of six balls bowled in cricket.
annotation.definitionFit: Overpaid means rewarded more than the work deserved.

entries.clue: Heads of financial institute enjoy stimulating team-building adventure holiday (6)

indicatorNotes.Heads of: the head of a word is its first letter

blocks.clueFragment: financial institute enjoy stimulating team-building adventure
blocks.note: first letters of the six words

annotation.surface: Bank bosses go on a corporate away-day full of bonding exercises.
annotation.walkthrough: Heads sounds like company bosses, which suits the corporate surface, but it means the first letter of each word.
annotation.definitionFit: A fiesta is a festive holiday, especially in Spain or Latin America.

entries.clue: Haughty setter’s promises about exercise regime’s start (9)

indicatorNotes.about: one thing about another goes round it
indicatorNotes.start: a word's start is its first letter

blocks.note: the setter is I, so setter's = I'M, I am
an IOU (I owe you) is a promise to pay

annotation.surface: A proud fitness instructor makes pledges about the first day of a workout plan.
annotation.walkthrough: The setter speaking of themself gives I'M; 'about' puts the two outer parts around the exercise and the first letter of 'regime'.
annotation.definitionFit: Imperious means arrogantly commanding, haughty.

entries.clue: Left creep quietly at home as essential part of plan (8)

blocks.note: to inch along is to creep slowly

annotation.surface: A sneaky figure slipping away from home is key to the scheme.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Creep' reads as a nasty person, but it is the verb, inch.
annotation.definitionFit: A linchpin is the pin through an axle, and so the part on which a whole plan depends.

entries.clue: Deny entrance following new rule finally (6)

indicatorNotes.following: what follows comes after, so GATE goes after N and E
indicatorNotes.finally: a word's final letter is its last

annotation.surface: A doorman refuses admission under a newly introduced policy.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue lists GATE first, but 'following' sends it to the end, behind N and E.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to rule a claim out or nullify it is to deny it.

entries.clue: School measurement getting knock back (7)

indicatorNotes.back: going back means running in reverse

blocks.note: a gram is a measure of weight
to ram is to knock into

annotation.surface: A school's test results take a hit.
annotation.walkthrough: A grammar is short for a grammar school, a British state secondary school that selects pupils by exam.
annotation.definitionFit: In Britain a grammar is a grammar school, a selective secondary school.

entries.clue: Small, magical creature in case is most crude (8)

blocks.note: S = small, as on clothing labels
an imp is a small mischievous sprite
lest = in case, for fear that

annotation.surface: A tiny fairy kept in a box looks very primitive.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In case' looks like a container instruction, but the two words together are one phrase meaning 'for fear that'.
annotation.definitionFit: Simplest can mean most basic or unrefined: most crude.

entries.clue: One getting away from European headland in South East (7)

indicatorNotes.in: one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: S = south; with the E below it forms the case holding CAPE

annotation.surface: A fugitive flees from a promontory on the south-east coast of Europe.
annotation.walkthrough: 'From' is only a link: the wordplay E plus S(CAPE)E is what the one getting away comes from.
annotation.definitionFit: The -ee suffix names the person the action concerns, here the one doing the getting away.

entries.clue: Signorina triumphs exhibiting hall (6)

indicatorNotes.exhibiting: to exhibit is to put on show, so the answer is on show inside the words

annotation.surface: An Italian young woman wins at an art show.
annotation.walkthrough: Signorina is Italian for Miss; the answer spans the join between the two words.
annotation.definitionFit: An atrium is a large open entrance hall.

entries.clue: Indifferent alien in charge following a direction (9)

indicatorNotes.following: what follows comes after, so ET and IC go after A and PATH

blocks.note: a path is a route or direction

annotation.surface: An unbothered space creature is put in command of a course of action.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue names the second half first; 'following' sends the alien and the in-charge piece after 'a direction'.
annotation.definitionFit: Apathetic means showing no interest, indifferent.

entries.clue: Dull house with unpleasant smell (2-3)

blocks.note: HO = house, as in estate agents' abbreviations
hum is British slang for a bad smell

annotation.surface: A boring home that smells bad.
annotation.walkthrough: A hum is British slang for a stink, as in 'there's a bit of a hum in here'.
annotation.definitionFit: Ho-hum means boringly ordinary, dull.

entries.clue: Explore recreation ground by church (5)

blocks.note: the rec is British shorthand for a recreation ground or park

annotation.surface: Go and look round the park beside the church.
annotation.walkthrough: Recce is British informal for reconnoitre, to scout out an area; the rec is a local public playing field.
annotation.definitionFit: British informal verb, short for reconnoitre: to scout out a place before acting.

entries.clue: Echo New York politician heard initially? (5)

indicatorNotes.initially: initially means at the start, so take the first letter

annotation.surface: Asks whether a New York politician's words came back as an echo.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Echo' looks like a verb or a sound, but it is the nymph of Greek myth who could only repeat others' words. The question mark marks Echo as one example of a nymph.
annotation.definitionFit: Echo was a nymph in Greek mythology, doomed to repeat the last words spoken to her.

entries.clue: I am on time, posh and spontaneous (9)

blocks.note: U = upper-class, a British label for posh usage

annotation.surface: Someone boasts of being punctual, well-bred and yet free-spirited.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On' looks like a positional instruction, but 'on time' is one phrase meaning punctual. U for posh comes from the 1950s U and non-U labels for upper-class speech.
annotation.definitionFit: Something impromptu is done on the spur of the moment, spontaneous.

entries.clue: Leaders of failing strip-mines welcoming revolutionary Islamic leader (5,9)

indicatorNotes.failing: something failing is breaking down, so the letters break up
indicatorNotes.welcoming: to welcome someone is to take them in
indicatorNotes.revolutionary: a revolution turns things round, so the word is reversed

blocks.note: an emir is a Muslim ruler; reversed it gives RIME, taken in after the P

annotation.surface: Bosses of collapsing open-cast mines take in a radical Muslim cleric.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leaders of failing strip-mines' tempts you to take first letters, but 'Leaders' alone is the definition; the rearranged STRIPMINES goes round RIME.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: heads of government are national leaders.
